inputs: story/structured_story.json + story/structured_story/ch001..ch012.json (paragraph text and scene paragraph_range used to place every event on the narrative axis)
_meta.scope: Faithful reading of the SOURCE (Lewis Carroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, ch001-ch012). No realistic-adaptation decision is taken here; open points are cross-referenced to events.json's realistic_adaptation_flags (rn-01 dream frame, rn-02 talking animals, rn-03 size changes) rather than repeated in full.
_meta.citation_format: chNNN#pMM or chNNN#pMM-pNN per bible/WRITE_RULES.md section 2

method.narrative_axis: Grouped by structured_story scene (46 scenes across ch001-ch012, in book reading order, order 1-46). Each event is placed in the scene containing its 'result' paragraph (the paragraph where its outcome actually lands); 6 of the 54 events physically start in one scene and land in the next (spans_from noted on the entry) because the source scene boundary falls mid-event. 4 scenes carry no event of their own because the event whose process they dramatize lands (and is therefore filed) in the following scene; each such scene still gets an entry with events: [] and a note explaining what happens there.
method.story_time_axis: One shared relative clock, T0 = ev0001 (the dream begins, 'a hot summer afternoon', ch001#p01-p02). Every event's own time_hint field in events.json already states its story-time relation to its predecessor (almost always 'continuous, immediately after'); this file carries that relation forward as the anchor, adds the two explicit elapsed-time markers the source itself gives (ch003#p19 and ch009#p36, both 'half an hour or so'), and tags each event's reality_layer (real_frame vs. dream) per the retroactive frame the source reveals at ev0053.
method.finding: Narrative order equals story-time order for the entire 54-event main sequence -- Carroll narrates strictly chronologically from ev0001 to ev0054 with zero chapter- or scene-level reordering. The only narrative-order/story-time mismatches in the book are the six embedded narrations listed in anachrony[] (verbal insets told by a character, nested inside a single frame-event's dialogue) and the two-layer dream status recorded in dream_frame. This is why the narrative[] and story_time[] axes below track each other 1:1 in sequence, and why anachrony[] is short rather than pervasive.

dream_frame.status: single retrospective dream frame; the source withholds the dream reading until the very end and only then confirms it (ev0053), per events.json realistic_adaptation_flags rn-01

real_world_open.note: Alice, drowsy on a hot afternoon beside her sister, is the last real-world state given before the White Rabbit runs by; the source never explicitly narrates her falling asleep -- the moment of falling asleep is only inferable retroactively from ev0053.

dream_span.note: Everything from the fall down the well to the pack of cards flying up at Alice (ev0002-ev0052) is, per ev0053, the content of Alice's dream. Narrated in strict real-time sequence as if diegetically real; nothing in the prose itself marks it as unreal until the waking.

waking.note: Alice wakes on the same bank, head in her sister's lap, dead leaves (the source's real-world echo of the flying cards) being brushed from her face; her sister remarks on 'what a long sleep' -- the only textual gesture at how much real time the nap took, left unquantified.

coda.note: Real-world frame continues (Alice has run off to tea) but immediately nests a second, smaller dream: the sister's own reverie, explicitly called 'this was her dream' at ch012#p67. See anachrony an-06.

dream_frame.open_for_realistic_adaptation: Whether to keep this exact dream frame, relocate it, or stage the whole thing ambiguously is deferred to Phase 2 (see events.json realistic_adaptation_flags rn-01); not decided here.

story_time_of_inset.basis: Told as a shape-poem in the third person ('Fury said to a mouse, that he met in the house...'), not in the first person as the Mouse's own remembered history, even though Alice asks for 'your history...why it is you hate [cats and dogs]' (ch003#p31). The source leaves it ambiguous whether this is the Mouse's own past experience retold as allegory or a traditional tale/fable it is reciting; no explicit anchor is given either way, so no story-time position is asserted here.

anachrony.note: Interrupted mid-recitation when Alice, distracted by the literal shape of the Mouse's tail, loses the thread (ch003#p33-p38); the Mouse leaves offended before finishing (ch003#p39-p42). See also story_graph.json foreshadowing fs-009.

anachrony.note: The text summarizes rather than replays the recap ('So Alice began telling them her adventures...') and does not requote it, so no new paragraphs need re-placing on the axes; it is flagged here purely because it is a narrated retelling-within-the-story of material the reader already saw in narrative order, the mirror image of a flashback. Alice's estimate of her own timeline appears immediately before it: 'it's no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then' (ch010#p50), i.e. she treats the dream's events as if they spanned at least from 'yesterday' -- a subjective-time remark the source does not reconcile with the single-afternoon real-world frame; noted, not treated as a conflict, since it is Alice's own dream-logic phrasing rather than an assertion about real elapsed time.

notes_for_downstream: The four events.json broken_chains (ev0039 missing cause, ev0038 missing leads_to, ev0014 missing cause, ev0052 missing leads_to) are causal/explanatory gaps in the source, not chronological-ordering contradictions (no dead-then-alive, no recognized-before-met, no age inversion), so they are not listed under conflicts[] above; they remain visible in this file via the story_time entries for ev0014 and ev0039, whose confidence is lowered accordingly.

character-growth / environment / costume / blocking: every event's reality_layer tag (real_frame vs. dream) tells you whether a given moment is inside the dream (ev0002-ev0052, the overwhelming majority) or the waking frame (ev0001, ev0053, ev0054) -- useful for any staging decision that needs to distinguish 'real Alice on the riverbank' from 'dreamed Alice in Wonderland'.

No two events in this book place the same character in mutually exclusive states at the same story-time position; the only recurring characters who might look inconsistent across chapters (Bill the Lizard: kicked up a chimney in ch004, then a jurorin ch011-ch012; the Duchess's baby, who becomes a pig in ch006) are consistently single-state at each of their own appearances -- verified against arc-bill-the-lizard and arc-duchess-household in story_graph.json.

This file does not make any realistic-adaptation decision (dream frame, talking animals, size changes) -- see events.json's realistic_adaptation_flags and story_graph.json's realism_notes for the open questions Phase 2 must rule on.
